result.summary: Telemachus reaches Eumaeus's hut, where Minerva restores Ulysses' true form and father and son are reunited and plan revenge on the suitors. Meanwhile the suitors learn Telemachus has escaped their ambush, debate killing him, and Penelope rebukes Antinous.

scenes.title: Telemachus arrives at the hut
scenes.summary: Telemachus is welcomed by Eumaeus and asks about the stranger. Ulysses, still disguised, rebukes him for tolerating the suitors.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus fears for his household and for the stranger's safety among the insolent suitors.

scenes.title: Telemachus sends Eumaeus to Penelope
scenes.summary: Telemachus explains his plight and sends Eumaeus to tell Penelope he is safe. Minerva appears to Ulysses and restores his youthful form.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must reveal himself and plan the suitors' destruction without being exposed.

scenes.title: Father and son reunited
scenes.summary: Ulysses convinces Telemachus of his identity. They weep, learn the suitors' numbers, and plan to hide the arms.
scenes.stakes: Two men face over a hundred suitors; failure means death.

scenes.title: The suitors learn of the return
scenes.summary: The ship from Pylos reaches harbour, messages reach Penelope, and the suitors debate how to kill Telemachus.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus's life is threatened; the suitors fear exile if he exposes them.

scenes.title: Penelope rebukes Antinous
scenes.summary: Amphinomus urges caution. Penelope confronts Antinous, and Eurymachus falsely reassures her.
scenes.stakes: Penelope's son is in danger and her household is being consumed.

scenes.title: Evening at the hut
scenes.summary: Minerva disguises Ulysses again as Eumaeus returns with his news, and they eat and sleep.
scenes.stakes: Eumaeus must not recognise Ulysses or the secret may be betrayed.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses reveals himself to his son.
Telemachus doubts the miraculous transformation, suspecting a god's trick.

analysis.text: Recognition and disguise: Ulysses' identity is revealed first to his son, and divine transformation makes the reunion possible.
The scene reflects the Greek ideals of hospitality and the duty to protect suppliants, which the suitors violate.

legacy.text: The father-son recognition scene became a model for later recognition scenes in literature.

fun_facts.text: Telemachus lists 108 suitors here, plus attendants, making the odds against the two men clear.

language_notes.text: "Were were" is a typographical slip in the source; read "were getting breakfast ready."
"Light of my eyes" is an affectionate idiom meaning someone dearly loved and precious.
The bed of Ulysses stands for his marriage; if Penelope remarried, his bed would be abandoned and empty.
Thesprotians lived in Epirus, northwest of Ithaca. Ulysses' invented tale placed him on a ship from there.
A suppliant is someone who seeks protection and mercy; Greek custom, guarded by Jove, required hosts to protect such people.
Ulysses asks whether Telemachus has no brothers to back him; a man was expected to rely on them in quarrels.
"Bane" means ruin or destroyer; Ulysses says he would be the death of the suitors.
Marauders are raiders who plunder; here the suitors, who consume Telemachus's wealth while courting his mother.
"Point blank" means bluntly and directly; Penelope neither refuses outright nor commits to remarrying.
"More's the pity" is an idiom meaning that is all the sadder.
Swineherd is Eumaeus's occupation: he keeps Ulysses' pigs.
"Station" means the farmstead or dwelling place of the swineherd, with its huts and yards.
A wand is the goddess's tool for transformation, here used to change Ulysses' appearance.
"Propitious" means favourably disposed, kindly. Telemachus promises sacrifice in exchange for the god's goodwill.
"Redoubtable" means formidable, inspiring awe or fear.
The Phaeacians were a seafaring people, famed for giving safe conveyance to strangers. They brought Ulysses home in Book 13.
Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus are islands near Ithaca. The suitors come from the neighbouring nobility. "Achaeans" here means Greeks.
"Exploit" is used in the sense of test or probe, here the women servants' loyalty. Telemachus repeats it in sentence 110.
"Compunction" means a pricking of conscience, so the suitors waste the estate without guilt.
"Prove" means test, put to the proof.
The presents are gifts Telemachus received as a guest in Pylos and Sparta; they are stored at Clytius's house, presumably a friend's home, for safekeeping.
"The House" means the palace of Ulysses, where Penelope lives and the suitors feast.
The "great wall that ran round the outer court" is the palace's boundary wall; the suitors step outside it to talk out of earshot.
The suitors had set an ambush for Telemachus in the strait between Ithaca and Samos, waiting to kill him on his return voyage.
"Our affair is never likely to come off" means their plan to win Penelope and the household will never succeed.
"Make our offers" refers to bridal gifts offered to a woman's family; the suitor offering the most, or favored by chance, would win her.
"Take counsel of the gods" means to seek the gods' guidance; "hold your hands" means to refrain from acting.
The "cloister" here is the roofed colonnade or covered court of the house, not a monastery; the "bearing-posts" are the pillars holding up its roof.
Suppliants were under Jove's protection. Harming those who sought refuge broke sacred custom, and Antinous's father had himself once been such a suppliant in Ulysses' house.
Penelope recalls an earlier event: Antinous's father joined Taphian raiders against the Thesprotians, Ithaca's allies, and was saved from the angry people by Ulysses.
"My spear shall be reddened with his blood" is Eurymachus's oath, but it means he will kill whoever harms Telemachus. The ambiguity hides his real intent.
"Clad him in his old clothes" means she restored his beggar's rags, reversing the earlier transformation in which he appeared as a handsome man to his son.
The suitors had set an ambush to kill Telemachus on his voyage home from Pylos; "to take me on my way home" refers to this plot.
"Those who had gone with you to Pylos" are Telemachus' crew, whom he sent ahead to the town while he went to the swineherd's hut.
"Boon" means a welcome blessing or gift; here sleep is a gift after the day's tensions.

context_notes.text: Telemachus had gone to Pylos, Nestor's city, to seek news of his father. Eumaeus feared the suitors' ambush might kill him.
Here the narrator addresses Eumaeus directly ("you answered"), a habit Homer uses to show affection for the swineherd.
Penelope was pressed to remarry. Her choice of the best suitor would give that man Ulysses' household.
Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus are islands near Ithaca; nobles from them are among Penelope's suitors.
Telemachus had gone to Pylos to seek news of his father from Nestor; he has just returned secretly.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is goddess of wisdom and war, and Ulysses' protector throughout the poem.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) has just touched Ulysses with her wand, transforming him from a ragged beggar into a vigorous, well-dressed man.
Ulysses left for Troy, and the war and his wanderings lasted twenty years in all.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods and Minerva is his daughter, goddess of wisdom and war. She is Ulysses' patron.
Hiding the arms means that the suitors will be unarmed when the fight comes.
Eurymachus is one of the leading suitors, known for smooth speech and cunning; he and Antinous are the main voices among them.
Amphinomus is a suitor, but the poem portrays him as comparatively decent and less eager for violence.
Telemachus can call an assembly of the Achaeans (the Ithacan people), where he could publicly accuse the suitors of plotting murder.
Dulichium was an island near Ithaca. Amphinomus, the most decent of the suitors, is shown to be better disposed than the rest.
Medon was a herald in Ulysses' household who served the suitors but remained loyal to Penelope's family, which is why he warned her.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Ulysses' protectress, and here sends Penelope to sleep, as she often does in the poem.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' divine patron. Her wand transforms his appearance, as earlier, so he can remain hidden from everyone but his son.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) was the god of roads and travellers, so a hill sacred to him, with a shrine or marker, suits a path into town.

literary_notes.text: The dogs' silence recognizes a friend; Ulysses' notice of it also hints at the coming recognition of father and son.
Eumaeus's joy is compared to a father's reunion with an only son, stressing how deeply he loves Telemachus.
Eumaeus kisses him as though Telemachus had returned from the dead, capturing the fear that he was lost.
Ulysses, speaking as a stranger, says what he would do if he were Ulysses, which he truly is; the audience knows.
The family's single line of sons shows how vulnerable Telemachus is, with no brothers or kin to defend him.
The dogs' scared whining shows the goddess's presence through animal reaction, since only Ulysses and the dogs perceive her.
Ulysses' renewed youth and clean clothes symbolize his restored identity and strength as he prepares to reclaim his house.
Ulysses' long-held tears show his self-control, a trait that defines him throughout the poem.
Telemachus rightly suspects divine involvement but wrongly doubts the truth. The audience knows Minerva did cause the change.
Father and son are compared to birds of prey robbed of their young, giving their shared grief a wild, raw intensity.
The claim that the suitors' reckoning is near anticipates the slaughter to come.
Eurymachus proposes sending a ship to recall the ambushers just as Amphinomus sees Telemachus's ship already in harbour, undercutting the suitors' plan.
Antinous speaks first and boldly, showing himself as the most ruthless suitor, bitter at the gods' protection of Telemachus.
Antinous fears exile from the people, while the audience knows a far worse fate approaches with Ulysses secretly at hand.
Antinous ends with a stark choice, murder and seizing the property or stopping the feasting, revealing how much greed drives the suitors.
Penelope sarcastically repeats Antinous's reputation as a wise speaker and counsellor, then denies it, exposing his wickedness by contrast.
Eurymachus's solemn promise to protect Telemachus is a lie, and the audience knows it, which makes his comforting words sinister.
The narrator openly exposes Eurymachus's deceit, guiding the reader's judgment of him and underlining the danger Telemachus faces.
Eumaeus guesses the armed men are the suitors, while Telemachus and the reader know more; his uncertainty heightens the sense of hidden knowledge.
Telemachus' secret smile shows him as shrewd and now a partner in his father's deception, no longer the naive youth.
